title: Wildlife Rehabilitation
short: Temporary treatment of injured, sick, or orphaned wild animals, with release as the goal. Permit-bound and focused on the individual animal.
bigPicture: Wildlife rehabilitation is the professional care of sick, injured, and orphaned wild animals with the aim of returning them to the wild. It is defined as much by law as by science: holding native wildlife requires a state permit, and migratory birds and certain species carry additional federal requirements. Two national organizations support the profession and jointly publish its standards, and there is a certification structure, but certification and licensure are separate things.

terms.definition: Professional care of sick, injured, or orphaned wild animals with the goal of returning them to the wild.
The legal authorization from a state agency, and for some species a federal one, that allows a person to hold native wildlife.
A voluntary professional credential earned by continuing education and examination; separate from a permit and not a substitute for one.
Rapid assessment on arrival to decide priority, treatment, and whether recovery to release is realistic.
An animal losing its natural wariness of humans, which usually makes release unsafe or impossible.
Another animal of the same species; raising young with conspecifics helps prevent habituation and misdirected imprinting.
Releasing an animal gradually with continued support such as supplemental food and a familiar enclosure.

focus.title: Intake, triage, and assessment
focus.description: Evaluating an animal on arrival, deciding what care is possible, and making honest judgments about prognosis and whether release is realistic.
focus.source: International Wildlife Rehabilitation Council (IWRC): how to become a wildlife rehabilitator

focus.title: Species-appropriate care
focus.description: Housing, diets, and handling that differ substantially by species and life stage, guided by published standards rather than improvisation.
focus.source: International Wildlife Rehabilitation Council (IWRC): how to become a wildlife rehabilitator

focus.title: Minimizing habituation
focus.description: Caring for an animal while limiting its association with humans, since an animal that loses its wariness cannot usually be released.

focus.title: Release and outcome
focus.description: Conditioning, timing, site selection, and post-release considerations, with release as the measure of success rather than survival in care.

questions.question: Can this animal recover well enough to survive in the wild?
questions.approach: Through intake examination against species-specific criteria, veterinary assessment, and honest judgment about function the animal will need after release.

questions.question: What does this species need at this life stage?
questions.approach: By working from published rehabilitation standards and species care protocols rather than improvising, especially for diet and housing of young animals.

questions.question: Is this animal orphaned, or should it be left alone?
questions.approach: By asking the finder about circumstances and duration, since many apparently abandoned young are being cared for and removing them causes the harm.

questions.question: How do we provide care without habituating the animal to people?
questions.approach: By minimizing contact and noise, using visual barriers and species-appropriate housing, and raising young with conspecifics wherever possible.

questions.question: Is release realistic, and if not, what is the right decision?
questions.approach: By assessing residual disability against what the animal needs to survive, and choosing between placement and euthanasia rather than indefinite holding.

questions.question: Where and when should this animal be released?
questions.approach: By matching site to species and season, considering the original capture location, habitat quality, and whether the animal is conditioned for release.

responsibilities: Perform intake, triage, and daily care under permit conditions.
Administer treatment in coordination with a veterinarian.
Maintain detailed records required by permitting agencies.
Handle public intake calls, education, and volunteer coordination.
knowledgeSkills: Species natural history, diets, and life stages
Triage, handling, and basic clinical technique
Zoonotic disease awareness and safety practice

variations.label: Certification is not a license
variations.description: the International Wildlife Rehabilitation Council (IWRC) offers Associate Wildlife Rehabilitator and Certified Wildlife Rehabilitator credentials, based on continuing education and an exam and renewable every two years. Neither one authorizes you to hold wildlife. The state permit does that, and in most places it requires apprenticeship under a licensed rehabilitator plus a relationship with a veterinarian.
variations.source: International Wildlife Rehabilitation Council (IWRC): certification questions and answers

variations.label: Standards exist
variations.description: IWRC and the National Wildlife Rehabilitators Association jointly publish standards covering ethics, species-specific care, housing, and disinfection, so this is not a field where practice is left to individual judgment.
variations.source: International Wildlife Rehabilitation Council (IWRC): how to become a wildlife rehabilitator

variations.label: Facility type
variations.description: Work ranges from large centers with veterinary staff to small home-based operations, with very different resources and daily rhythms.

variations.label: Species focus
variations.description: Many rehabilitators specialize in raptors, songbirds, small mammals, marine mammals, or reptiles, and permits are often species-specific.

realities: Paid positions are limited; much of the field runs on volunteers and seasonal staff at nonprofit centers.
The legal framework is strict and varies by state, and unpermitted care of native wildlife is illegal.
Mortality is a routine part of the work, and euthanasia decisions are frequent.
Intake volume is highly seasonal, with spring and summer far busier than the rest of the year.
